ingredients.item: Flaky salt , sliced scallion , toasted sesame seeds

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: Sear dry scallops, undisturbed, 90 seconds — no baste yet, because butter burns where the paste would scorch. The sear happens in plain fat and the flavor comes after.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: lift one: a deep golden-brown crust on the bottom face. No crust, back down — and if the pan was smoking hard, it ran a notch hot for butter's tolerance.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Flip, and baste the seared faces now — brush or spoon the doenjang-butter over each scallop, 60–90 seconds more, off the fire while the centers still carry the faintest translucence at the very core (carryover finishes them on the platter).
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the basted tops should sit glossy and foamy-gold. A test scallop cut in half: opaque to within a few millimeters of the center, buttery, just springy. Fully opaque-through at the pan means slightly over — edible, but the next batch pulls 15 seconds sooner.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Flaky salt, scallion, sesame; serve immediately, off the shared platter, one or two per diner with rice beside.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: eating test: crust, then the sweet scallop burst, then doenjang's savory depth arriving on the butter — the three arriving in that order is the build working. Salty-only means the baste ran heavy on paste; a teaspoon, not a tablespoon, is the ratio.

storageNotes: Scallops are cook-and-eat; raw ones keep 24 hours on ice in the fridge, no marinade. The baste keeps a week refrigerated and improves.
Variations: a drop of gochujang into the baste for heat; the same baste on king oyster mushroom slices for the table's vegetarians; stirred into rice at the end — the leftover baste's best job.
